c.tagline: Renaissance beauty carved in stone and light

emergency.note: 112 is the universal EU number; 113 (state police) and 118 (ambulance) also work, and English-speaking operators are usually available.

hood_landmark.Oltrarno: Palazzo Pitti and the Boboli Gardens
hood_landmark.Santa Croce: Basilica di Santa Croce with Michelangelo's tomb
hood_landmark.San Lorenzo: Basilica di San Lorenzo and the Medici Chapels
hood_landmark.Santa Maria Novella: Basilica of Santa Maria Novella's striped marble façade

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing around the Duomo, Ponte Vecchio and Santa Maria Novella station

hood_desc: Oltrarno is the artisan quarter across the Arno, full of workshops, leather makers, wine bars and a genuine local feel, ideal for travelers seeking authentic, less touristy Florence.
Santa Croce surrounds the great Franciscan basilica and Michelangelo's tomb, a lively area of leather markets, trattorias and nightlife, great for sightseers and evening buzz.
San Lorenzo centers on the bustling Mercato Centrale food hall and street market near the Medici chapels, a busy, budget-friendly base popular with foodies.
Santa Maria Novella wraps around the main train station and its namesake church, a convenient, well-connected hub handy for arrivals and first-time visitors.
lodging: B&B Hotel Firenze Pitti Palace al Ponte Vecchio

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink; it can taste mineral-heavy but poses no health risk.

transit.pay: A single ticket costs 1.70 EUR (~US$2) and is valid 90 minutes on trams and buses; buy from tram-stop machines, tabacchi shops or the at bus app. On trams you can simply tap a contactless bank card at the on-board validators. Buy bus tickets before boarding and validate them.
transit.hours: Trams run about 5am-12:30am (until ~2am Friday-Saturday); most buses run 6am-9pm.

transit.m: Tram T2 to the city center (20 min)
Volainbus shuttle to Santa Maria Novella station (20 min)

food.name: Bistecca alla fiorentina
food.desc: Thick T-bone of Chianina beef grilled over embers, served rare and sold by weight. Ordering it well done is not really an option.

places.name: Buca Lapi
places.note: Poster-lined 1880 cellar under Palazzo Antinori; dinner only, reserve.

places.name: Trattoria Mario
places.note: Lunch-only shared-table institution behind the Mercato Centrale.

places.name: Trattoria dall'Oste
places.note: Steak specialist listed among the world's top steak restaurants in 2024.

food.name: Lampredotto
food.desc: The fourth stomach of the cow, simmered in broth and stuffed into a roll dipped in the cooking liquid, with salsa verde and chilli oil.

places.name: Nerbone
places.note: Market kiosk since 1872, famous for its wet-dipped panino; go before 1pm.

places.name: Tripperia Sergio Pollini
places.note: Van on Via dei Macci run by Sergio and son for nearly thirty years.

places.name: Il Trippaio del Porcellino
places.note: Cart by the bronze boar statue, handy for a cheap central lunch.

food.name: Schiacciata sandwich
food.desc: Crisp olive-oil flatbread split and piled with Tuscan cured meats, pecorino, truffle cream or artichoke. Florence's answer to fast food.

places.name: All'Antico Vinaio
places.note: The famous one on Via dei Neri; huge sandwiches and even huger queues.

places.name: Da Vinattieri
places.note: Alley hole-in-the-wall near Dante's house, also does lampredotto.

places.name: I' Girone de' Ghiotti
places.note: Locals' pick with quality Tuscan salumi and far shorter waits.

food.name: Ribollita
food.desc: Thick winter soup of cavolo nero, cannellini beans and vegetables, thickened with stale bread and reboiled the next day, finished with olive oil.

places.name: Trattoria Sabatino
places.note: Family-run canteen outside Porta San Frediano, very cheap and very local.

places.name: Trattoria Sergio Gozzi
places.note: Lunch-only trattoria near the market serving a rotating Tuscan menu.

places.name: La Casalinga
places.note: Oltrarno home-cooking stalwart; expect to share the room with regulars.

food.name: Pappa al pomodoro and crostini toscani
food.desc: Bread-and-tomato porridge drenched in olive oil, and toasts spread with warm chicken liver pate. The standard Tuscan opening act.

places.name: Trattoria Sostanza
places.note: 1869 dining room known as Il Troia; cash, shared tables, two sittings.

places.name: Il Santo Bevitore
places.note: Modern Tuscan cooking and a deep wine list in a converted Oltrarno cellar.

places.name: Trattoria Cammillo
places.note: Long-running Borgo San Jacopo trattoria mixing classics with the odd curveball.

food.name: Gelato
food.desc: Florence claims to have invented gelato; look for muted natural colours, metal tubs with lids and seasonal fruit flavours.

places.name: Vivoli
places.note: Open since 1929, served in cups only; the rice and coffee flavours are classics.

places.name: Gelateria dei Neri
places.note: Consistently rated among the city's best, with strong dark chocolate.

places.name: La Carraia
places.note: By the bridge of the same name, generous portions at low prices.

food.name: Chianti Classico
food.desc: Sangiovese red from the hills between Florence and Siena, marked by a black rooster seal. Made for Tuscan meat and bread dishes.

places.name: Le Volpi e l'Uva
places.note: Tiny wine bar off Ponte Vecchio with small-grower pours and cheese plates.

places.name: Enoteca Pitti Gola e Cantina
places.note: Sangiovese-focused list opposite the palace; knowledgeable owners.

places.name: Casa del Vino
places.note: Wood-panelled counter behind the market for a glass and a crostino.

food.name: Negroni
food.desc: Gin, Campari and sweet vermouth in equal parts, created in Florence around 1919 when a count asked for his Americano to be made stronger.

places.name: Caffe Giacosa
places.note: The bar credited with the drink's invention, now part of Roberto Cavalli's cafe.

places.name: Rivoire
places.note: 1872 cafe with terrace tables facing Palazzo Vecchio; also famed for hot chocolate.

places.name: Manifattura
places.note: All-Italian-spirits cocktail bar in a 1930s-styled room.

landmarks: Florence Cathedral (Duomo di Santa Maria del Fiore)
Brunelleschi's massive red-tiled dome dominates the skyline and is one of the most photographed sights in Italy.
Giotto's Campanile
An intricately decorated Gothic bell tower next to the Duomo, offering panoramic views of the city.
Florence Baptistery
Famous for Lorenzo Ghiberti's gilded bronze 'Gates of Paradise' doors, a Renaissance masterpiece.
Ponte Vecchio
A medieval stone bridge lined with jewelry shops, iconic for its reflection over the Arno River, especially at sunset.
Uffizi Gallery
One of the world's great art museums, housing masterpieces by Botticelli and da Vinci in a stunning Renaissance building.
Piazza della Signoria & Palazzo Vecchio
Florence's historic civic square, filled with Renaissance sculptures and dominated by the fortress-like Palazzo Vecchio tower.
Piazzale Michelangelo
A hilltop terrace offering the classic postcard panorama of Florence's skyline and the Arno valley.
Basilica di Santa Croce
A grand Gothic church and burial site of Michelangelo and Galileo, known for its ornate marble facade.
Pitti Palace & Boboli Gardens
A monumental Renaissance palace with sprawling formal gardens, offering elegant architecture and sweeping views.
Basilica of San Miniato al Monte
A striking green-and-white marble-façade Romanesque church perched above the city with sweeping views.

train.note: Since the December 2025 timetable change the Vienna sleeper runs via Graz and a new direct EuroCity links Florence with Zurich. Both Nightjets (which continue to/from Rome) use Firenze Campo di Marte station, not Santa Maria Novella. Domestic high-speed trains are run by Trenitalia and competitor Italo (italotreno.com).

bus.note: Most long-distance coaches leave from Villa Costanza (tram T1 from the centre) or the bus terminal by Santa Maria Novella station. Itabus (itabus.it) covers domestic routes.

ferry.note: Florence is inland with no port. The nearest ferry port is Livorno (about 1h30 by train), with sailings to Corsica and Sardinia run by Corsica Ferries and Moby.

half.name: Siena
half.blurb: Medieval hill city built around the shell-shaped Piazza del Campo and a striped marble cathedral.

half.name: Pisa
half.blurb: Home to the famous Leaning Tower rising beside a cathedral on the grassy Field of Miracles.

half.name: Lucca
half.blurb: Charming walled town ringed by tree-topped Renaissance ramparts perfect for cycling and strolling.

half.name: San Gimignano
half.blurb: Hilltop town bristling with medieval stone towers, surrounded by vineyards and famed for white wine.

half.name: Chianti
half.blurb: Rolling wine country of vineyards, olive groves and stone villages between Florence and Siena.

full.name: Cinque Terre
full.blurb: Five colorful fishing villages clinging to dramatic cliffs along the rugged Ligurian coastline.
